sink: node:fs writeFileSync(filePath, ...) at src/gnfd/services/object.ts:445
why: objectName (fully caller-controlled per the tool's zod schema, src/gnfd/tools/storage.ts:291) is concatenated into the local write path via path.join(targetPath, objectName) with zero sanitization (no path.basename, no containment check). path.join normalizes '..' segments, so objectName='../../etc/cron.d/x' (or similar) escapes targetPath entirely, e.g. path.join('/home/user/downloads','../../etc/cron.d/x') resolves outside downloads. Even with no targetPath, the fallback `path.join(process.cwd(), \`tmp-${objectName}\`)` (line 420) does not meaningfully block this: because the 'tmp-..' pseudo-segment is itself consumed by the first '..', a second '..' still pops a real parent directory (verified by manual path.normalize segment-stack trace), so cwd can still be escaped with objectName containing 2+ '../' segments. The remote object need only exist under an attacker-controlled/public Greenfield bucket the caller is told to download from (bucketName is an arbitrary caller string too) — the attacker does not need write access to the MCP host at all. Impact is an arbitrary local file write (integrity), not mere robustness/DoS.

analyzeNip19Entity (utils/conversion.ts) only bech32-decodes the input and returns a formatted string; relay fields in decoded nprofile/nevent/naddr are filtered to ws(s):// with no creds and are never used to open a connection.

convertNip19Entity (utils/conversion.ts) re-encodes between NIP-19 formats; relays/author/kind/identifier are only embedded in the encoded output string via snstr's encodeProfile/encodeEvent/encodeAddress and filtered through isValidRelayUrl, never used to connect anywhere.
profile/profile-tools.ts createKeypair() calls snstr generateKeypair() and returns the new key to the caller who explicitly asked for one; no logging or persistence of the generated key was found.
event/event-tools.ts createNostrEvent() only builds and returns an unsigned event object via snstr's createEvent; no network or filesystem sink.
note/note-tools.ts createNote() derives the pubkey from the caller-supplied privateKey and returns an unsigned kind-1 event object; no publish or logging occurs.

dm/dm-tools.ts decryptDmNip44() calls snstr decryptDirectMessage() using the caller's own privateKey on a caller-supplied gift-wrap event; snstr's NIP-44 implementation uses ChaCha20 with random 32-byte nonce and constant-time HMAC verification (node_modules/snstr 0.3.1), no crypto misuse found.

dm/dm-tools.ts decryptNip04() calls snstr decryptNIP04() with the caller's own privateKey; snstr AES-256-CBC decrypt (node_modules/snstr 0.3.1, nip04/index.js) parses IV from the wire format and requires it to be 16 bytes -- standard NIP-04, no static IV or key reuse introduced by this wrapper.

dm/dm-tools.ts decryptNip44() calls snstr decryptNIP44() with caller's own key; verified snstr's NIP-44 v2 decrypt (node_modules/snstr 0.3.1) uses HKDF-derived per-message keys and constantTimeEqual MAC check, no misuse.
social/social-tools.ts deleteEvent() signs a kind-5 deletion request with the caller's own privateKey and publishes it to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose.

dm/dm-tools.ts encryptNip04() calls snstr encryptNIP04(); verified snstr's implementation (node_modules/snstr 0.3.1, nip04/index.js) generates a fresh random 16-byte IV via randomBytes() per call -- no static IV/ECB.

dm/dm-tools.ts encryptNip44() calls snstr encryptNIP44(); verified snstr's NIP-44 v2 encrypt (node_modules/snstr 0.3.1) generates a fresh random 32-byte nonce via randomBytes() per call and derives per-message ChaCha20/HMAC keys via HKDF -- no misuse.

social/social-tools.ts follow() updates the caller's own kind-3 contact list (signed with caller's privateKey) and publishes to caller-specified relays; relayHint/petname are only stored as inert tag values, never used as a connection target.
index.ts getAllZaps handler only queries relays for kind 9735 events and formats them via processZapReceipt/formatZapReceipt (zap/zap-tools.ts); no write or fetch sink.

dm/dm-tools.ts getDmConversationNip04() queries relays for kind-4 events between caller and peer and decrypts with the caller's own privateKey via snstr decryptNIP04; advertised purpose, no crypto misuse (see decryptNip04 finding).
dm/dm-tools.ts getDmInboxNip44() queries relays for gift-wrap (kind 1059) events tagged to the caller and decrypts with the caller's own privateKey via snstr decryptDirectMessage; advertised purpose.
social/social-tools.ts exports getFollowing as a direct alias of getContactList; identical read-only behavior.
note/note-tools.ts / index.ts getKind1Notes handler only queries relays for kind-1 events by author and formats them via formatNote; no sink.
index.ts getLongFormNotes handler queries relays for kind-30023 events and formats tag metadata for display; no sink.
note/note-tools.ts formatProfile + index.ts getProfile handler only fetch and JSON.parse the target's kind-0 metadata event for display; no sink.

index.ts getSentZaps handler queries relays for kind-9735 receipts with #P tag matching the pubkey and formats them; no sink.

note/note-tools.ts postAnonymousNote() generates a fresh one-time keypair via snstr generateKeypair() purely in-memory to sign the note, then publishes to caller-specified relays; the ephemeral key is not logged, persisted, or returned to the caller.
profile/profile-tools.ts postNote() signs a kind-1 note with the caller's own privateKey and publishes to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose.

event/event-tools.ts publishNostrEvent() opens a raw `new WebSocket(relayUrl)` per caller-supplied relay string with no protocol allowlist, but this is plain 'connect where I'm told' (ws lib rejects non-ws(s) URL schemes) with no extra twist such as file access, matching the explicit anti-false-positive rule for relay URL args.
note/note-tools.ts publishNote() takes a caller-supplied already-signed event and publishes it to caller-specified relays via pool.publish; no additional twist beyond connecting to the given relay.

event/event-tools.ts queryEvents()/queryEventsOverWebSocket() opens `new WebSocket(relayUrl)` for each caller-supplied relay string with no scheme allowlist, same as publishNostrEvent -- plain 'connect to the relay I gave you', excluded per the anti-false-positive rule.
social/social-tools.ts reactToEvent() signs a kind-7 reaction with the caller's own privateKey to a caller-specified target event and publishes to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose.

social/social-tools.ts replyToEvent() signs a kind-1 reply (using snstr createReplyTags/parseThreadReferences for NIP-10 tags) with the caller's own privateKey and publishes to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose.
social/social-tools.ts repostEvent() signs a kind-6 repost with the caller's own privateKey and publishes to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose.

sink: fetch(lnurl) and fetch(callbackUrlString) -- outbound HTTP GET to a URL built from the zap target's own Nostr profile (lud16/lud06) or its bech32-decoded domain, not from a caller-supplied URL argument
guard: partial: isValidUrl() (zap/zap-tools.ts:614) only checks protocol is http/https; there is no check against private/loopback/link-local/metadata-service IP ranges or DNS rebinding, and lud16 addresses are only prefixed with https:// (no host allowlist)
why: prepareAnonymousZap() (called from sendAnonymousZap) resolves the caller-supplied `target` pubkey/event to that entity's author, fetches that author's kind-0 profile from relays, and extracts the lud16/lud06 field verbatim from the profile JSON to build an LNURL that the server itself fetches twice (initial LNURL-pay query and the payment callback). Since any Nostr profile is self-published and unauthenticated, an attacker can set lud16 to any host (e.g. an internal/metadata address) and have the MCP server's process make outbound requests to it merely by being picked as a zap target -- this is a genuine SSRF vector distinct from the caller directly supplying a relay/URL argument.
contract: Prepare an anonymous zap to a profile or event

why: dm/dm-tools.ts sendDmNip04() encrypts with the caller's own privateKey via snstr encryptNIP04 (random IV verified) and publishes the kind-4 event to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose.

relay/relay-tools.ts setRelayList() validates every relayList.url with isRelayUrl() (must be ws:// or wss://, relay/relay-tools.ts:13-20) before including it in the published NIP-65 event, then signs with the caller's own privateKey and publishes to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose with an effective format guard.

event/event-tools.ts signNostrEvent() only hashes and signs a caller-supplied event with the caller's own privateKey and returns the signed event; it also verifies the derived pubkey matches the event's pubkey before signing. No network or disk sink.
note/note-tools.ts signNote() verifies the derived pubkey matches the note event's pubkey, then signs with the caller's own privateKey and returns the signed note; no network or disk sink.

social/social-tools.ts unfollow() updates the caller's own kind-3 contact list (signed with caller's privateKey) removing the target pubkey and publishes to caller-specified relays; advertised purpose.

No input parameters; returns a static server-info string built entirely from local config.
Only a boolean 'force' flag; builds an auth URL from static config constants, no caller data reaches any sink.

sink: unencoded ID concatenated into a Microsoft Graph API URL path passed whole to https.request(), which applies dot-segment (../) normalization at the wire level
why: eventId is a free-form caller-controlled string (no format/encoding). utils/graph-api.js builds the final URL by splitting the already-interpolated endpoint on '/' and encoding each resulting segment, but encodeURIComponent never touches '.' characters, so a value like 'X/../../messages/YYY' still splits into real path segments including literal '..' tokens; verified in utils/graph-api.js:36-38 that split happens after $-interpolation, and confirmed with a local Node http reproduction (v22.23.2) that https.request(url,...) normalizes those dot-segments before the request line is sent, letting a crafted eventId redirect this calendar-only tool's POST into a different same-token Graph endpoint (e.g. /v1.0/messages/YYY/cancel).
contract: Cancels a calendar event

why: No arguments; only reads the local token cache and returns a fixed status string.
subject/start/end/attendees/body are placed only into a JSON POST body sent to the caller's own /me/events endpoint; none of them are used to build a URL path or command.
parentFolder is resolved server-side to a folder ID via getFolderIdByName (API lookup); the ID used in the resulting endpoint is not directly the caller string.
All fields are placed into a JSON rule body posted to a fixed me/mailFolders/inbox/messageRules endpoint; moveToFolder is resolved to an ID via API lookup, not interpolated into a URL.

sink: unencoded ID concatenated into a Microsoft Graph API URL path passed whole to https.request(), which normalizes ../ dot-segments at the wire level
why: Same mechanism as cancel-event/delete-event: eventId is caller-controlled free text, merged into the endpoint template before utils/graph-api.js splits on '/' and per-segment-encodes, so literal '..' segments inside eventId survive encoding and are later resolved away by URL normalization before the request is sent, letting a crafted eventId redirect the POST to a different Graph resource under the caller's own token.
contract: Declines a calendar event

why: email/delete.js wraps emailId in encodeURIComponent() directly (before template interpolation), which encodes any literal '/' in the ID so it cannot become an extra path segment -- verified this defeats the dot-segment injection that affects the unencoded-ID tools in this repo.

sink: unencoded ID used verbatim as the full Graph API URL path for a DELETE request
why: eventId is caller-controlled and unencoded before template interpolation. Reproduced with a local http server (matching this exact https.request(url,{method}) pattern, Node v22.23.2) that eventId='../../messages/YYY' turns the constructed path into the literal wire path '/v1.0/messages/YYY'; applied here, a crafted eventId lets a DELETE intended only for a calendar event instead delete an arbitrary same-token Graph resource, which is a genuine authorization-scope violation, not mere robustness.
contract: Deletes a calendar event

why: to/cc/bcc/subject/body go only into a JSON POST body sent to the fixed me/messages endpoint; no path/command construction from caller input.

ruleName is only compared client-side (rule.displayName === ruleName) to select a rule object already fetched from the API; the ID actually placed in the PATCH endpoint (rule.id) comes from that API response, not from caller input.

sink: unencoded ID interpolated into a Power Automate Flow API path; power-automate/flow-api.js builds the final URL with new URL(fullUrl), which normalizes ../ dot-segments before extracting options.path for https.request
why: environmentId is caller-controlled free text with zero encoding anywhere in the chain (flow-api.js does not even per-segment-encode, unlike the Graph client). Reproduced with Node's URL constructor (node -e, v22.23.2) that environmentId='../../../connections/evilConn' turns the intended path into '/connections/evilConn/flows' on the same host, using the caller's Flow bearer token -- redirecting a fleet/environment-scoped listing into an arbitrary sibling Flow API resource.
contract: List flows in a Power Platform environment

why: Calls a fixed '/environments' path with no caller-supplied ID; no injectable argument reaches the URL.

sink: two unencoded IDs interpolated into a Flow API path that is later normalized by new URL() before the request is sent
why: Same unguarded interpolation as flow-list; either environmentId or flowId containing '../' segments is normalized away by new URL(fullUrl) in power-automate/flow-api.js (verified: node v22.23.2 new URL() reproduction), letting the caller redirect this GET to a different Flow API resource under the same access token.
contract: Get run history for a flow

sink: two unencoded IDs interpolated into a Flow API path, normalized by new URL() before the POST is sent (with attacker-controlled 'inputs' as the JSON body)
why: Same mechanism as flow-list/flow-list-runs. Because this handler issues a POST with a caller-controlled JSON body ('inputs'), a crafted environmentId/flowId could redirect the POST to a different Flow API endpoint that accepts that verb, combining path redirection with attacker-supplied payload delivery under the caller's own Flow token.
contract: Trigger a manual flow run

sink: two unencoded IDs interpolated into a Flow API path, normalized by new URL() before the POST (start/stop) is sent
why: Same unguarded interpolation as the other Power Automate tools; a crafted environmentId/flowId is normalized by new URL(fullUrl) in flow-api.js, letting a call meant only to start/stop one specific flow redirect its POST to a different Flow API path with the caller's own token.
contract: Enable or disable a flow

why: folder resolves through resolveFolderPath/getFolderIdByName against the caller's own mailbox; the underlying OData $filter string-interpolation in folder-utils.js is unescaped but only ever queries the caller's own mail folders, not a cross-account boundary.
startDateTime/endDateTime/count are parsed as Date/number and placed only in query parameters against the caller's own me/calendarView; no path or command construction from raw strings.
Only boolean display-formatting flags (includeItemCounts/includeChildren); the actual endpoint (me/mailFolders) is fixed.

sink: unencoded ID concatenated into a Graph API URL path used for a POST, later normalized by https.request's URL parsing
why: Each emailId is taken directly from the caller-supplied comma-separated emailIds string (only trimmed, never encodeURIComponent'd), unlike email/read.js and email/mark-as-read.js in the very same codebase which do encode -- confirmed by direct comparison of the three files. A crafted ID containing '../' segments is normalized by the underlying https.request(url) call, letting the caller redirect the POST to a different Graph resource than the target message, still mutating it via the caller's own token.

why: 'path' is a hierarchical folder path by design (expected to contain '/'), used only to address the caller's own OneDrive root; 'name' goes only into the JSON body, not the URL.

sink: unencoded item ID used as the Graph API URL path for the initial GET (and subsequently for the DELETE, via itemInfo.id from that response)
why: itemId is an opaque caller-supplied string per the tool's own schema, never encoded. Reproduced (node v22.23.2, local http server mirroring the exact https.request(url) call) that itemId='../../messages/YYY' turns the constructed path into a different resource type than a OneDrive item, driving the subsequent delete decision (isFolder/itemName) and the actual DELETE call on the resolved ID from that redirected response -- exceeding the tool's OneDrive-only scope.

sink: unencoded item ID used as the Graph API URL path, later normalized by https.request's URL parsing before the request is sent
why: itemId is caller-controlled and unencoded. Empirically reproduced (node v22.23.2, http server matching the exact https.request(url) pattern used here) that itemId='../../messages/YYY' makes the wire-level request path resolve to a different resource than the intended drive item, so a crafted itemId can make this OneDrive-only tool fetch (and return a '@microsoft.graph.downloadUrl'-shaped view of) a different Graph resource such as a message, using the caller's own bearer token.

why: 'path' is a hierarchical OneDrive path by design; normalization only ever redirects within the caller's own root:/...:/children addressing scheme and lands on malformed/non-existent endpoints rather than a clean alternate resource (the fixed 'root:' / ':children' template segments make a clean redirect impractical, unlike the opaque-ID tools).
query is passed through encodeURIComponent() before being embedded in the search(q='...') endpoint, preventing it from introducing extra path structure.

sink: unencoded item ID (when supplied directly, resolvedItemId===itemId) used in a Graph API URL path for a POST that creates a sharing link
why: When the caller supplies itemId directly (the tool's own schema offers itemId as an alternative to path), it is used completely unencoded. Same reproducible mechanism as onedrive-download/onedrive-delete: a crafted itemId with '../' segments is normalized away by the https.request(url) call, letting the caller redirect the POST that creates an (anonymous, by default) sharing link to a different Graph resource than intended -- a confidentiality-relevant redirection since the tool's whole purpose is exposing a link to whatever resource the ID resolves to.
contract: Create a sharing link for a file or folder in OneDrive

why: 'path' is a hierarchical destination path by design; content is sent as the PUT body, not used to build the URL.

Same pattern as onedrive-upload: 'path' is a hierarchical destination path used only to address the caller's own drive root for the createUploadSession call; content is streamed as chunk bodies to the returned uploadUrl, not path-interpolated.
emailId is wrapped in encodeURIComponent() before being placed in the endpoint; includeRawHtml is a boolean only affecting whether raw HTML is echoed back (no sink).

query/from/to/subject are interpolated unescaped into a KQL $search string or OData $filter, a real but effect-limited mechanism since it only ever queries the caller's own mailbox -- no cross-account or cross-resource-type escape is possible through $search/$filter syntax the way it is through raw URL path concatenation.
to/cc/bcc/subject/body/importance are placed only into a JSON POST body sent to the fixed me/sendMail endpoint; no path/command construction from caller input.
entity_name/entity_type only drive in-memory lookups against cached FPL bootstrap data (name/position matching), never a path, command, or query sink.
player_name is used only to look up a player id in cached bootstrap data before fetching that player's fixtures from the FPL public API.
All filter/sort arguments (position, team, price/points thresholds, sort_by) only index into in-memory dicts/lists of cached player data; no injectable sink.

player_names and metrics only select entries/fields from cached bootstrap data for comparison; no execution or path/query sink.

num_gameweeks (int) only bounds a loop over cached fixture/gameweek data.

gameweek_id/player_ids/limit only select/filter data already fetched from the fixed FPL live-scores endpoint; no injectable sink.

excerpt: if (!absolutePath.startsWith(rootDir)) { throw new Error(`Invalid file path...`); }
sink: fs.writeFile(validatedPath, document.content, 'utf-8') in DocumentStorage.saveDocumentToCustomPath (document-storage.ts:291), called from the save_document tool with the caller-supplied filePath
guard: bypassable: rootDir is `${cwd}/documents` with no trailing separator; validatePath only does a raw string startsWith(rootDir) check after path.normalize, so a relative or absolute path whose final directory name merely starts with the literal substring 'documents' (e.g. 'documents-evil/x.md' or an absolute '<cwd>/documentsSHADOW/x.md') satisfies the check and writes outside the intended documents/ tree; normalize does correctly collapse '..' first, so full filesystem escape beyond the project root is not reachable, only sibling-directory escape
why: save_document's optional filePath flows straight into saveDocumentToCustomPath -> validateCustomPath -> validatePath, whose only containment check is a bare string prefix comparison without a path separator boundary; I confirmed the sibling-directory bypass is concrete (documents-x/evil.md passes) even though normalize blocks classic '../' escapes to arbitrary absolute locations.

sink: fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf-8') reached via LocalFileSystem.readFile -> FileUtils.readFile (src/utils/storage/LocalFileSystem.ts:67-69, src/utils/FileUtils.ts:52-59) with no path sanitization anywhere in the chain
guard: bypassable: filename is joined into memoryBankDir with zero validation (no '..' check, no path.resolve+startsWith containment); I verified with a standalone `node -e` script that LocalFileSystem re-joins the already-normalized filePath onto the server's fixed launch-time projectPath (path.join does not treat a leading '/' as a root reset), so a filename with enough leading '../' segments (path.normalize silently clamps excess '..' at the filesystem root) followed by a target like '.env' or 'package.json' reads that file from anywhere in the server's project root, escaping the intended memory-bank/ subfolder
why: There is no allow-list, containment check, or rejection of '..' in MemoryBankManager.readFile, LocalFileSystem, or FileUtils.readFile; my traced path.join experiment (memoryBankDir='<proj>/memory-bank', filename='../../../../package.json' -> intermediate '/package.json' -> re-joined to '<proj>/package.json') confirms the tool can read arbitrary files in the project root outside memory-bank/ (e.g. .env, config with secrets), even though the accidental double path.join prevents escaping the project root entirely.

sink: fs.writeFile(filePath, content) reached via LocalFileSystem.writeFile -> FileUtils.writeFile (src/utils/storage/LocalFileSystem.ts:77-79, src/utils/FileUtils.ts:68-75) with no path sanitization
guard: bypassable: identical unsanitized path.join(memoryBankDir, filename) as read_memory_bank_file; the only transform applied to filename is a cosmetic camelCase->kebab-case regex, never a traversal check; I verified with `node -e` that filename='../../../../package.json' collapses through memoryBankDir past the filesystem root (path.normalize clamps rather than erroring) and, once re-joined onto the server's fixed baseDir by LocalFileSystem, resolves to '<projectRoot>/package.json'
why: handleWriteMemoryBankFile passes the raw caller filename straight through to memoryBankManager.writeFile with no validation; the practical effect, confirmed by the path.join trace, is that a caller can overwrite arbitrary existing files anywhere in the project root (package.json, source files, .env, CI config) instead of being confined to the memory-bank/ subfolder -- a real integrity impact beyond the tool's advertised scope, even though the same double-join quirk prevents escaping the project root entirely.

sink: caller string value is embedded, single-quoted, into a KEY='value' line of a hand-built Horizons batch input file that is POSTed as multipart form data to https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons_file.api
guard: bypassable: the intended escaping `.replace(/'/g, "\'")` is a no-op in JavaScript -- "\'" inside a double-quoted string literal is just the single character "'", so every embedded quote is replaced with itself. A value such as COMMAND="499'\nSTOP_TIME='2030-01-01" closes the quoted field early and injects an extra KEY=VALUE directive line into the batch file sent to JPL.
why: Traced the full hop: args (Record<string, any>, not runtime-validated by any zod schema before this handler runs) -> formattedArgs entries -> broken replace() -> fileContent -> multipart 'input' field -> axios.post to the real JPL Horizons file API. contract: "JPL Horizons - Solar system objects ephemeris data (File Input)"

The written content (gpxData) is fetched from Strava using the caller's own token, but the destination path is fully attacker-controlled, giving an arbitrary local file write (bounded only by the fixed '.gpx' suffix and process file permissions).

why: tools/register-tools.js registerDeployLocalFolderTool only checks that folderPath is a non-empty string, then calls deploy({files:[folderPath],...}). Whenever the direct/no-Cloud-Build path is taken (deployWithZip, attempted first via deployer.js's canDeployWithoutBuild) or a docker-compose file is detected in the folder (deployCompose, which unconditionally calls prepareSourceDirectory), lib/deployment/source-processor.js's prepareSourceDirectory() runs `fsp.stat(file)`; if it is a directory it runs `execAsync(`cp -R "${file}/." "${tempDir}/"`)` via node:child_process exec, which spawns /bin/sh -c on the fully interpolated string. Because `file` is the raw folderPath with no escaping, any folder path containing a literal double-quote followed by shell syntax (e.g. a directory actually named `/tmp/x"; touch /tmp/pwned; echo "`) breaks out of the quoted argument and runs arbitrary shell commands with the privileges of the MCP server process. fs.stat/exec do not shell-parse the path themselves, so the only requirement for exploitation is that such a path exists on disk and is passed verbatim as folderPath -- the schema places no restriction on the string's shape. This is a real, unguarded shell-metacharacter injection, not just a robustness issue.
contract: Deploy a local folder to Cloud Run. Takes an absolute folder path from the local filesystem that will be deployed.

sink: used verbatim as the entry name inside a zip archive that is uploaded to a GCS bucket and later unpacked by Google Cloud Build / Cloud Run's buildpacks
dep_evidence: null
why: tools/register-tools.js registerDeployFileContentsTool only checks that each file has non-empty content; the filename string (which the tool's own description says can be a path like 'src/index.js' or 'data/config.json') flows unmodified into archiver's archive.append({name: file.filename}) with no rejection of '..' segments or absolute paths, so a filename like '../../malicious' would be written into the zip under that literal traversal path. Whether this is exploitable depends entirely on how Google's Cloud Build / buildpacks source-extraction unpacks the archive server-side, which is outside this repo and cannot be inspected from source, so I cannot confirm a concrete bypass or rule one out -- this is a real, unguarded mechanism in this repo's own code but the impact is unproven, matching Tier B rather than Tier A.
contract: Deploy files to Cloud Run by providing their contents directly. Takes an array of file objects containing filename and content.

why: tools/register-tools.js registerGetServiceTool forwards project/region/service to lib/cloud-api/run.js getService(), which builds a Cloud Run Admin API resource name via runClient.servicePath(project, location, serviceId) (the client library's own path builder, not string concatenation into a URL or shell) and calls the gRPC getService RPC; only returns data about the caller's own project.

tools/register-tools.js registerGetServiceLogTool forwards project/region/service to lib/cloud-api/run.js getServiceLogs(), which builds a Cloud Logging filter string by directly interpolating serviceId/location without escaping (`resource.labels.service_name="${serviceId}"`). This is an unguarded filter-string injection in this repo's own code, but the loggingClient is already scoped to the caller-supplied `projectId`, and Cloud Logging IAM (roles/logging.viewer etc.) is granted at the project/bucket level, not per Cloud Run service -- so breaking out of the service_name/location clause only lets the query see logs the caller's own token can already read within that project by simply calling this same tool again with a different `service`/`region` argument. There is no confidentiality boundary the injection uniquely crosses, so it does not meet the 'genuine security property' bar for a finding.
tools/register-tools.js registerListProjectsTool has inputSchema: {} (no parameters); it calls listProjects(options.accessToken) with only the server's own configured access token.

tools/register-tools.js registerListServicesTool forwards only `project` (a string) to lib/cloud-api/run.js listServices(), which uses runClient.locationPath(projectId, location) (client-library path builder) per discovered location and calls the gRPC listServices RPC; only lists the caller's own project's services.
Only deletes an entry from the in-process ActionRecorder sessions Map keyed by caller sessionId; no file/command/URL sink reached.

excerpt: const outputPath = path.isAbsolute(mergedOptions.outputPath) ? mergedOptions.outputPath : path.join(workspaceRoot, mergedOptions.outputPath);
sink: fs.mkdir(outputPath) creates the directory tree; the same path is later used by end_codegen_session's fs.writeFile to write a generated .spec.ts file there
why: options.outputPath is a caller-supplied string (schema explicitly invites 'use absolute path') with zero validation; it is stored on the session and used verbatim to mkdir and then (in end_codegen_session) to write an attacker-influenced file into any directory the process can reach. Impact is limited to writing a fixed-suffix .spec.ts file (filename pattern is sanitized), and the schema documents absolute-path usage as intended for a local dev tool, so this is Tier B rather than A.
contract: Directory path where generated tests will be saved (use absolute path)

why: Looks up and returns an in-memory session object by sessionId; no external sink.

selector is passed to Playwright's page.click(); no other caller-controlled data reaches a sink.

script is passed straight to page.evaluate(), i.e. arbitrary JS execution inside the browser page's JS context — but that is exactly the tool's declared purpose ('Execute JavaScript in the browser console'), and execution is confined to the Playwright-controlled browser page, not the Node host process. id/url are stored/used only to key an in-memory Promise map and call Playwright's own page.waitForResponse(url) pattern matcher; no external sink.
selector/value are passed to Playwright's page.fill(); no code/command/path interpretation.

Takes no arguments; calls Playwright's page.goForward().

excerpt: await page.goto(args.url, { timeout: args.timeout || 30000, waitUntil: args.waitUntil || "load" });
sink: Playwright Chromium's page.goto() with a caller-controlled URL, with no scheme allow-list, so file:// URIs are navigated to and their content becomes part of the loaded page
why: url is the raw string from the tool call and reaches page.goto() with no scheme check anywhere in navigation.ts or tools.ts. Beyond plain 'fetch a remote URL' this also lets the agent load file:// URIs, exposing local filesystem content, which can then be exfiltrated by chaining with playwright_get_visible_html/text or playwright_screenshot. Tier B because it needs a second tool call to extract/exfiltrate the content and the schema only documents 'a URL' generically rather than an explicit local-file-read capability.
contract: URL to navigate to the website specified

why: Performs an HTTP PATCH to the caller-given URL with caller-given body; plain HTTP client behaviour, the tool's advertised purpose.
Performs an HTTP POST to the caller-given URL with caller-given body; plain HTTP client behaviour, the tool's advertised purpose.
key/selector are passed to Playwright's page.focus()/keyboard.press(); no injection sink.

sink: page.pdf({ path }) writes the rendered PDF to the resolved filesystem path with no directory restriction or traversal check
why: outputPath and filename are caller-supplied strings (schema literally says 'Directory path where PDF will be saved') fed straight into path.resolve() with no allow-listing, so a caller can make the process write a PDF to any absolute path it has permission for, including via '../' segments in filename. This is an arbitrary-file-write primitive, but the schema documents free-form absolute-path usage as intended for this local dev tool, so Tier B.
contract: Save the current page as a PDF file

excerpt: const downloadsDir = args.downloadsDir || defaultDownloadsPath; ... const outputPath = path.join(downloadsDir, filename);
sink: fs.mkdirSync(downloadsDir, {recursive:true}) then page.screenshot({path: outputPath}) write a PNG/JPEG to the caller-chosen directory/filename
why: downloadsDir is used verbatim as the write directory (created recursively if missing) and args.name is concatenated into the filename with no traversal sanitization, so the tool can be made to create directories and write image files to arbitrary paths on disk. Schema documents downloadsDir as a free-form 'custom downloads directory path', so this matches the tool's intended flexibility for a local dev tool; Tier B.
contract: Take a screenshot of the current page or a specific element

why: selector/value are passed to Playwright's page.selectOption(); no injection sink.

contract: Absolute path to the file to upload

param: n/a (leak occurs on every call regardless of arguments)
sink: Returns the live DOLPHINSCHEDULER_API_KEY value (config.api_key) verbatim in the tool result to whoever invoked the tool
why: This tool takes no security-relevant argument -- the vulnerability is that any caller able to invoke it at all gets the raw configured API credential back in cleartext (api_key_value), when a boolean like the already-present has_api_key would fully serve the stated 'check settings' purpose. That credential then flows into the MCP client / LLM context (transcripts, logs, possibly a third-party model) with no authorization check of any kind, and is the same Token header used to authenticate every other write-capable tool in this server, so its disclosure is a genuine confidentiality/authorization failure (also fits CWE-522/CWE-306).
contract: Check the current environment settings for DolphinScheduler API

sink: Overwrites the process-wide Config singleton's api_url, which client.py then uses as the base URL (via string concatenation, url = f"{config.api_url}/{path}") for every subsequent tool call in the same running server, including attaching the 'Token' auth header when an api_key is configured
why: api_url is a plain caller-supplied string per this tool's own schema, with no validation, allow-list, or confirmation step, and is stored process-wide (also into the OS environment) so it silently redirects all later tool calls -- and their Authorization/Token header carrying the real DolphinScheduler API key -- to any attacker-chosen host. A caller (or a prompt-injected agent that is induced to call this one tool) can therefore both exfiltrate the configured API credential and have every subsequent create/update/delete call silently routed to a rogue server instead of the real DolphinScheduler instance. Every hop (schema -> Config().api_url setter -> client.request()'s URL/header construction) was read and there is no guard anywhere in the chain.
contract: 更新DolphinScheduler API连接设置 (update DolphinScheduler API connection settings)

why: Forwards collection id and content ids straight to client.addContentsToCollections, a GraphQL mutation against the caller's own Graphlit project.
prompt string is passed verbatim to client.askGraphlit(prompt), a remote GraphQL/LLM call on the Graphlit platform; the JSON message is only returned as text, never locally interpreted or executed.
All boolean/enum flags are used to build Specification/Workflow objects sent via upsertSpecification/upsertWorkflow/updateProject GraphQL mutations on the caller's own project; no local sink.
name and contents array are passed directly into client.createCollection, a GraphQL mutation on the caller's own project.
id is passed straight to client.deleteCollection(id), a GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project resource.
limit builds a CollectionFilter passed to client.deleteAllCollections, a bulk GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project; no path/command surface.
id is passed straight to client.deleteContent(id), a GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project resource.
contentType/fileType/limit build a ContentFilter passed to client.deleteAllContents, a bulk GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project.
id is passed straight to client.deleteConversation(id), a GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project resource.
limit builds a ConversationFilter passed to client.deleteAllConversations, a bulk GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project.
id is passed straight to client.deleteFeed(id), a GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project resource.
feedType/limit build a FeedFilter passed to client.deleteAllFeeds, a bulk GraphQL mutation scoped to the caller's own project.

id is used only to fetch the caller's own already-ingested content's imageUri via client.getContent, then that URI and optional prompt are forwarded to client.describeImage, a remote vision-LLM call; no local file/URL fetch.

prompt and url are forwarded verbatim to client.describeImage; the image URL is fetched by Graphlit's remote vision-LLM service, not by this process, and it's a plain fetch-what-you're-told with no additional twist (no local resolution, no allow-list bypass).

text, schema and prompt are forwarded to client.extractText, which runs the LLM extraction on the Graphlit backend; the schema string is only used as a remote LLM tool schema, not locally parsed/executed.
folderId/readLimit/recurring are placed into a createFeed GraphQL mutation with Box OAuth creds read from env; the Box API traversal happens entirely on Graphlit's backend.
channelName/readLimit are placed into a createFeed GraphQL mutation with the bot token read from env; Discord API access happens on Graphlit's backend.
path/readLimit are placed into a createFeed GraphQL mutation with Dropbox creds read from env; Dropbox API access happens on Graphlit's backend.

dep_evidence: node_modules/graphlit-client v1.0.20260111002, dist/client.js:1065 ingestEncodedFile() only wraps a GraphQL mutation (Documents.IngestEncodedFile) with the given name/data/mimeType — it performs no local path validation and never touches the filesystem itself, so the file read is entirely unguarded local code in tools.ts.
why: The declared schema takes an arbitrary string filePath with zero validation (no restriction to a workspace/allow-listed directory, no traversal check, no symlink check) and passes it straight to fs.readFileSync before uploading the contents to a persistent remote knowledge base. contract: Accepts the path to the file in the local filesystem. Can use for storing *large* long-term textual memories or the output from LLM or other tools as content resources.

sink: a caller-supplied 'COPY (...) TO PROGRAM '<os-command>'' statement is classified DQL/LOW risk and executed against the Postgres connection via postgres_client.execute_statement
guard: partial: classify_statement()'s CopyStmt special case only inspects stmt_node.is_from (COPY FROM=write vs COPY TO=read) and never checks stmt_node.is_program, so 'COPY (SELECT 1) TO PROGRAM '<cmd>'' (is_from=False, is_program=True) is misclassified as an ordinary low-risk export and is always allowed, even in default SAFE mode; the DB-level READ ONLY transaction that genuinely blocks INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL in SAFE mode (asyncpg Transaction, 'query += " READ ONLY"' in transaction.py) does not stop COPY TO PROGRAM either, since it does not modify the database itself
dep_evidence: pglast 7.3 installed at .venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/pglast/ast.py:1433 defines CopyStmt with a distinct 'is_program': 'bool' slot separate from 'is_from', proving the field the target ignores is exposed by the parser it uses; asyncpg (installed, version per repo lockfile) transaction.py appends 'READ ONLY' to the START TRANSACTION statement only when readonly=True, confirmed by static read of transaction.py
why: execute_postgresql's whole purpose is to run caller-supplied SQL, and ordinary writes/DDL are genuinely blocked in SAFE mode by both the pglast-based classifier and a real asyncpg READ ONLY transaction (verified in code) -- but COPY's risk classification only looks at direction (is_from), not at is_program, so a COPY ... TO PROGRAM statement bypasses the entire safety system and runs an OS command via the Postgres server without ever needing live_dangerously/UNSAFE mode. Actual impact depends on the connecting Postgres role holding COPY-to-program privilege (superuser or pg_execute_server_program membership), which is a deployment fact this repo cannot confirm, hence Tier B.
contract: SAFETY SYSTEM: ... LOW RISK: Read operations (SELECT, EXPLAIN) - allowed in SAFE mode ... The database client starts in SAFE mode by default for safety

guard: bypassable: SQLValidator defines validate_schema_name()/validate_table_name() which reject spaces/empty strings, but grep across supabase_mcp/ shows these are never called anywhere in the execution path (only referenced from tests/services/database/sql/test_sql_validator.py) -- get_table_schema_query() calls plain str.replace() with zero escaping. A value like table="x' UNION SELECT column_name,data_type,'t',NULL,1,NULL,NULL,NULL,'f' FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='auth' -- " still parses as a single SelectStmt, which SQLSafetyConfig always classifies LOW risk, so it executes even in default SAFE mode without ever needing live_dangerously.
why: schema_name/table are declared as plain strings in the tool's own signature and are string-spliced directly into quoted SQL literals with no escaping or allowlisting; because the final query still parses as one SELECT statement, the safety manager's risk-based gate (which only looks at statement type, not content) always treats it as low-risk and permits it regardless of safety mode, giving a full read-oriented SQL injection into arbitrary schemas/tables.

param: none (IPAPI_API_TOKEN is operator configuration, not a caller-supplied argument)
sink: writes the full outbound request URL (with the API token embedded as a ?key= query parameter, see src/utils/transport.util.ts fetchIpApi) plus the raw JSON response body to a file under /tmp/mcp/<project-name>/, created via recursive mkdirSync and written with fs.writeFileSync's default (world-readable) mode
why: fetchIpApi unconditionally appends key=<IPAPI_API_TOKEN> to the request URL whenever a token is configured (regardless of includeExtendedData), and that exact URL string is passed straight into saveRawResponse -> buildResponseContent -> fs.writeFileSync with no redaction. On a shared/multi-user host, any other local user can list /tmp/mcp/<project>/ and read the token out of the plaintext log file. This fires automatically on every call when a token is configured -- no malicious argument is needed -- which is why it is Tier B (config-dependent) rather than Tier A (no caller-controlled argument drives the leak).
contract: Powered by ip-api.com.

why: The compiled entrypoint is src/index.ts per tsconfig (rootDir/include src/**/*); topic is only interpolated into plain-text Google search query strings typed into a headless-browser search box (src/deep-research.ts), and subsequent URLs visited come from Google's own extracted result links, not from topic directly; no path/command/eval sink is reachable from the caller-controlled argument, and grepping the whole src tree found no exec/spawn/eval/new Function anywhere in this repo.

Each query is typed into Google's own search box via Puppeteer (no shell/URL built from the raw string); the only local filesystem write (src/parallel-search.ts saveResults) builds its filename via query.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '_'), which strips every character outside [a-z0-9] including '/', '\\' and '.', so path traversal via the query argument is not possible, and outputDir is not exposed in the tool's inputSchema in src/index.ts at all (only 'queries' and 'maxParallel' are) -- it is fixed to a server-side default under os.tmpdir().

sink: utils.compress_log_file() opens log_path for read and writes '<dir>/<name>_no_screenshots.json', '<dir>/<name>_compressed.gz' and a screenshots directory into os.path.dirname(log_path), i.e. whatever directory the caller names
why: log_path is expanduser'd/abspath'd with no directory allowlist, then compress_log_file() (src/nova_mcp_server/utils.py:582-712) reads it as JSON and writes derivative files (including base64-decoded screenshot bytes) into the same directory; this lets a caller make the server read and write files anywhere it has permissions, beyond the log directories the tool's own docstring implies.
contract: The absolute path to the log file to compress. This should be a path to a JSON log file generated by Nova Act

why: actions_end.end_session_action() only looks session_id up as a dict key in active_sessions and calls nova_instance.close()/pop(); the string never reaches a filesystem, shell, or eval sink.

actions_execute.execute_session_action_async() looks session_id up in active_sessions and passes task/instructions straight into nova_instance.act(); this is a natural-language instruction interpreted by Amazon's Nova Act SDK/browser agent, not executed locally as code or a shell command.

sink: open(file_path, "rb") reads and returns the full contents (optionally base64-encoded) of any path the process can read
why: file_path is expanduser'd/abspath'd with zero directory restriction and no extension allowlist, so the tool can read any file readable by the server process (e.g. ~/.ssh/id_rsa, .env secrets), not just the 'log files, screenshots, and other assets' its own description names; there is no guard to bypass, it simply has none.
contract: Retrieves the contents of a file from the server, with optional base64 encoding. Primarily used to access log files, screenshots, and other assets generated during browser automation.

why: actions_inspect._inspect_browser_async() only uses session_id as an active_sessions lookup key and globs *.html/*.json inside the server-computed logs_dir (not attacker-supplied); no caller-controlled path component.
session_listing.list_browser_sessions() takes no arguments and just returns a sanitized copy of the active_sessions registry (session_manager.list_active_sessions()).

sink: Path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates the directory tree for base_log_path, then this path is passed as logs_directory= to NovaAct(), redirecting the SDK's HTML/JSON/screenshot log writes there
why: The caller-controlled optional session_id argument to start_session (declared in the tool's own function signature, browser_control.py:37) becomes effective_session_id and is interpolated unsanitized into a single f-string path component; because it can contain '/' and '..' segments, a value like '../../../../tmp/evil' makes Path.mkdir(parents=True) create directories outside the intended tempfile.gettempdir() scratch area, and the resulting arbitrary path is then handed to the Nova Act SDK as its logs_directory for that session -- a genuine path-traversal write primitive with no sanitization of session_id anywhere in the call chain (verified via grep: session_id is never regex-checked or basename-stripped before use).
contract: Starts and initializes a new browser session controlled by Nova Act, navigating to the specified URL. Returns session details including a unique `session_id` required for other browser tools.

sink: gzip.open()/open() reads and returns the full contents of any path the process can read, decompressing .gz files and otherwise reading the file verbatim
why: compressed_path is expanduser'd/abspath'd with no directory restriction; the tool's own docstring admits it 'will also handle non-compressed files', i.e. arbitrary paths, and there is no guard limiting it to a logs/screenshots directory, so it can disclose any file readable by the server process.
contract: Retrieves and displays the contents of a compressed log file (.gz) previously created by the compress_logs tool. ... the tool will also handle non-compressed files.

sink: open(html_file_path).read() returns the file's raw content tagged as {"type": "html", "html": ...} content for the MCP client to render
why: When html_path is supplied directly (as opposed to session_id-based discovery), it is used with no directory restriction and no extension check beyond os.path.isfile, letting the caller read any file the process can access and have it returned/rendered as HTML content; the session_id branch is properly scoped via _normalize_logs_dir but the direct-path branch bypasses that scoping entirely.
contract: Provide either a session_id to automatically find the most recent HTML log for that session, or html_path to directly specify a log file path.

sink: ultralytics YOLO(model_path) -> nn/tasks.py torch_safe_load() -> torch.load(file, map_location='cpu') without weights_only by default (arbitrary pickle deserialization of the checkpoint)
guard: bypassable: get_model_path() does `Path("models") / model_name` then only checks `.exists()`; pathlib discards the 'models' prefix entirely when model_name is an absolute path (e.g. model_name='/tmp/evil.pt'), so any pre-existing file anywhere on disk can be loaded. PathAccessMiddleware does not help: it only intercepts arguments literally named 'path' or ending in '_path', and 'model_name' matches neither.
dep_evidence: .venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/ultralytics-8.4.153.dist-info; nn/tasks.py lines 1802-1852: torch_safe_load(weight, safe_only=None) defaults safe_only=SAFE_LOAD (an env-gated flag, off unless ULTRALYTICS_SAFE_LOAD is set) and when safe_only is False calls torch_load(file, map_location='cpu') with no weights_only=True restriction, i.e. full unrestricted pickle load
why: model_name is a declared, caller-controlled argument; every hop (get_model_path -> Path join -> exists check -> YOLO(model_path) -> torch_safe_load -> torch.load) was read, and the installed ultralytics version confirms unsafe pickle loading is the default unless an env var most users never set is enabled. Loading an attacker-supplied .pt file this way can execute arbitrary code during unpickling. Requires the malicious file to already exist at the target path (e.g. planted via another write-capable tool or already present), so it's a real exploit but with a precondition.
contract: This tool requires pre-downloaded models. Use the download-yolo-models command to download models before using this tool.

why: Tool schema declares zero parameters ({}), so there is no caller-controlled input at all; it just calls leetCodeApi.daily() with a hardcoded GraphQL query.

titleSlug flows to LeetCodeGlobalService/CNService.fetchProblem -> leetCodeApi.problem(slug), which passes slug only as the GraphQL variable $titleSlug (node_modules/leetcode-query lib/index.js:464-470, v2.0.1, query template 'query ($titleSlug: String!) {...}') -- never string-concatenated into the query text, and the resulting JSON is only returned to the caller (no file/URL/shell sink).

topicId (Global) or slug (CN) is passed solely as a bound GraphQL variable to SOLUTION_ARTICLE_DETAIL_QUERY ($topicId/$slug placeholders in src/leetcode/graphql/{global,cn}/solution-article-detail.ts); no string interpolation into the query and no other sink for the value.

username/limit are bound as GraphQL variables in the inline query in leetcode-global-service.ts:112-131 ($username, $limit) or, on CN, passed to leetCodeApi.recent_submissions(username) which uses a parameterized query (node_modules/leetcode-query lib/index.js:704-713, v2.0.1); no injection path.

username/limit go to leetCodeApi.recent_submissions(username, limit), whose library query template binds them as $username/$limit GraphQL variables (node_modules/leetcode-query lib/index.js:144,348-355, v2.0.1); returned data is only serialized back to the caller.

username is bound as the $username GraphQL variable in leetCodeApi.user_contest_info (node_modules/leetcode-query lib/index.js:126,329-336 Global and 681-692 CN); attended is used only as a local boolean filter over the already-fetched array (leetcode-global-service.ts:154-166), never a sink.

username is passed to leetCodeApi.user(username), bound as the $username GraphQL variable in the library's profile query template (node_modules/leetcode-query lib/index.js:141,311-318 Global, 622,663-670 CN, v2.0.1); no other use of the value.

questionSlug/limit/skip/orderBy/userInput/tagSlugs are all placed into the `variables` object passed to leetCodeApi.graphql() and bound via declared GraphQL variables ($questionSlug,$orderBy,$userInput,$tagSlugs,$skip,$first) in src/leetcode/graphql/{global,cn}/solution-articles.ts; none are spliced into the query string, and orderBy/tags come from constrained schema types (tagSlugs/userInput are free strings but only ever used as GraphQL filter variables, not a sink).

category/difficulty/tags are zod-enum constrained; searchKeywords/limit/offset are placed in a `filters`/`variables` object bound via GraphQL variables ($categorySlug,$limit,$skip,$filters) in src/leetcode/graphql/{global,cn}/search-problems.ts -- no string interpolation into the GraphQL query text and no other sink.

spenderAddress and amount are caller-controlled but this is the exact declared purpose of an ERC20 approve tool (owner explicitly authorizes a spender via their own wallet), with no additional sink or bypass beyond viem's standard writeContract call.

Performs a read-only eth_call (client.readContract) against a caller-supplied token/spender/owner address on an RPC endpoint chosen from the fixed rpcUrlMap, no state change or arbitrary host reachable.

sink: services/wallet.ts signMessage() calls account.signMessage({message}) using the env-configured private key/mnemonic with zero validation, confirmation, or allowlisting of the message content before producing a valid signature from a fund-controlling key.
why: The tool signs whatever arbitrary string the caller supplies with the real wallet key (services/wallet.ts:96-105), with no display, confirmation step, or restriction on message content; because personal_sign signatures can be used for off-chain authentication/authorization (e.g. SIWE) elsewhere, an agent tricked into calling this with attacker-chosen content could produce a usable signed authorization without the wallet owner ever reviewing what was signed.
contract: Sign an arbitrary message using the configured wallet. Useful for authentication (SIWE), meta-transactions, and off-chain signatures.

excerpt: const signature = await services.signTypedData(domain, types, primaryType, message);
sink: services/wallet.ts signTypedData() calls account.signTypedData({domain,types,primaryType,message}) using the env-configured key, with domain/types/message parsed straight from caller JSON and no semantic validation (e.g. no check on verifyingContract, no amount/allowance caps, no confirmation).
why: domain, types, primaryType and message are fully attacker/caller-controlled JSON strings that get signed as-is by the real wallet key with no allowlist of verifyingContract, no inspection of primaryType (e.g. an ERC-2612 Permit granting unlimited allowance to an arbitrary spender), and no confirmation step; the tool's own description explicitly lists 'permit signatures' as a use case, so blind-signing an arbitrary permit is a direct path to fund loss once the resulting signature is used on-chain.
contract: Sign structured data (EIP-712) using the configured wallet. Used for gasless transactions, meta-transactions, permit signatures, and protocol-specific signatures.

sink: id is concatenated raw into the REST path passed to plankaRequest(), which builds the final URL with `new URL(path, baseUrl)`; WHATWG URL dot-segment resolution lets a value like "../projects/<targetId>" strip the "/api/boards" prefix and retarget the request at a completely different Planka resource (e.g. /api/projects/<targetId>) while keeping the caller-chosen HTTP method (DELETE for delete_board).
why: index.ts:41-161 passes args.id straight to boards.deleteBoard/updateBoard/getBoard with no format check; common/utils.ts:110-112 builds the URL via native `new URL()`, which normalizes ".." segments per RFC3986 before the request is sent, so id="../projects/X" turns a delete_board call into a DELETE against /api/projects/X. No encodeURIComponent, UUID regex, or path allow-list exists anywhere in the repo (grepped for encodeURIComponent/uuid/sanitize/validateId with zero hits) and the DELETE path never validates the response shape, so the request completes regardless.
contract: Manage projects and boards with various operations

excerpt: This server does not perform human confirmation. A boolean tool argument is not human approval (an agent can set it). The MCP client must gate this privileged side-effect before calling the tool.
sink: send_message()->_send_message_to_recipient()/_send_message_direct() (messages.py:661,892,1610) executes an AppleScript `send` unconditionally as soon as the tool function is called -- there is no confirmation flag, allow-list, rate limit, or any other in-code gate between the arguments and the external side effect of actually sending a message via Messages.app.
why: The AppleScript string-injection surface itself is effectively guarded (escape_applescript, messages.py:59-79, escapes backslash/quote/CR/LF/tab/U+2028/U+2029 in the correct order, and is covered by dedicated injection tests in tests/test_messages.py). The remaining gap is structural: the tool's own docstring explicitly admits the server performs zero human-confirmation check and defers all gating to the calling MCP client, and grep of send_message()/_send_message_to_recipient()/_send_message_direct()/_send_message_sms() confirms there is truly no such check anywhere in the code path -- any caller (including an LLM acting on attacker-influenced context) can cause an irreversible, real-world message send with no server-side control. This exceeds what a reasonable caller would expect from a tool advertised as having 'an external side effect' with a stated gating requirement, so it is filed as Tier B (mechanism is real and the advertised purpose itself is to send messages, but the total absence of any authorization/confirmation check on a destructive/irreversible external action goes beyond bare purpose-fulfillment) rather than Tier A, since the risk is contingent on the calling client/agent's own behavior, which this repo cannot control.
contract: This server does not perform human confirmation... The MCP client must gate this privileged side-effect before calling the tool.

sink: folderPath (any absolute path, no allowlist) is recursively walked with fs.readdirSync/fs.statSync/fs.readFileSync in addDirectoryToZip (lines 45 and 54), zipped, uploaded to OSS via uploadZipToOSS, then published to both staging and production via createRoutineCodeDeployment, making every file under that path reachable at the returned public access URL.
why: I traced path from the tool schema through addDirectoryToZip's fs.readdirSync/fs.readFileSync calls (lines 45-54) to the zip buffer that gets uploaded to OSS and then deployed to a public production URL (lines 204-334). There is no check that the path stays inside a project or allowed directory, and the recursive walk does not skip dotfiles, so a caller (or an LLM agent tricked via prompt injection into supplying a sensitive path such as a home directory or credentials folder) causes local files to be packaged and served publicly, which is a genuine confidentiality impact beyond the tool's stated purpose of publishing a specific static-site folder.

sink: html is escaped and spliced into a JS template literal (const html = `${html}`;) at line 44 that becomes the source of the deployed Edge Routine, uploaded via uploadCodeToOSS and published to staging/production via publishRoutineCodeVersion.
guard: bypassable: a raw backslash immediately followed by a backtick in the html value survives the two replace() calls (lines 41-42) as an escaped-backslash-plus-unescaped-backtick sequence, which closes the template literal early; the remaining attacker-controlled text becomes live JavaScript in the deployed worker instead of inert HTML text.
why: I traced html from the schema at line 40 through the escaping at lines 41-42 into the code template at line 44 that is uploaded and executed by the Edge Routine runtime. The escaping only neutralizes a lone backtick or dollar sign; it does not account for a backslash already present in the input immediately before a backtick, so that two-byte sequence defeats the escaping and lets injected text execute as code, which is a real code-injection primitive distinct from the tool's advertised purpose of deploying literal HTML markup.

sink: When mode is simple, route.ts calls transferRouteToRuleString(route) (src/utils/helpers.ts line 100), which splices the caller-supplied host/uriPath substrings directly, unescaped, into a double-quoted rule-language expression (http.host eq "HOST" and http.request.uri.path eq "PATH") that is then sent as the rule field to Aliyun's createRoutineRoute API.
guard: partial: a quote character in the route value is not escaped before being embedded in the generated rule string, letting a caller alter the intended match clause (e.g. broaden or corrupt which host/path pattern the rule matches); however the same rule field can already be supplied verbatim by using mode=custom, so this does not cross a privilege boundary the caller couldn't already reach directly.
why: I read transferRouteToRuleString in src/utils/helpers.ts fully: it does string interpolation of host/uriPath into a quoted DSL expression with no quote-escaping, so a route value containing a double-quote can change the semantics of the resulting match rule sent to Aliyun. I mark this Tier B rather than A because mode=custom already lets the caller pass an arbitrary rule string directly, so the injection does not grant capability beyond what the tool already exposes, and the concrete impact of a malformed rule on Aliyun's matching engine could not be verified without executing the API.

Exploitability additionally requires the connected DB account to have the FILE privilege and a permissive secure_file_priv setting, which cannot be confirmed statically (project's own config falls back to a root DB user by default, making this plausible but unconfirmed) -- this unconfirmed environment precondition is what keeps it at Tier B rather than A. sink: pypandoc invokes each resolved path in `filters` as an executable Pandoc filter (pandoc --filter <path>) during conversion
why: This is a genuine two-call RCE chain fully contained within this one tool. Call 1: output_file is completely unrestricted (any absolute path; only its parent directory is mkdir'd) and, for a basic output_format like markdown/plain/txt, the caller's own `contents` string is written verbatim to that path -- so a caller can write an arbitrary script (e.g. Python) to any writable location, such as output_file='/tmp/x.py' with contents=<malicious code>. Call 2: that same path is then passed in `filters`; resolve_filter_path() only checks the path exists (os.path.isabs -> used as-is, or existence-checked in a few fallback locations) with no allowlist, no check that it originated from a trusted source, and no restriction on what the 'filter' actually does -- pandoc executes it as part of the conversion pipeline. The 'filters' feature is a secondary, advanced capability layered onto a document-conversion tool, not the tool's core declared identity, so this does not fall under the advertised-purpose exclusion the way an explicit code-execution tool would.

sink: execAsync(<command string>) -- runs through a shell
guard: bypassable: code.replace(/"/g,'\\"') blindly escapes every quote regardless of a preceding backslash
why: Running caller-supplied Babashka code is this tool's stated purpose, so that alone is not the finding -- the finding is that the quoting meant to confine `code` inside the -e "..." shell argument is bypassable, letting a caller break out into arbitrary OS shell commands (not just babashka code). Concretely: code ending in a literal backslash immediately before an embedded quote (raw chars ...\\") becomes ...\\\\" after the replace (the pre-existing backslash plus the replacement's escaped quote = two backslashes then a bare quote). Bash reads \\\\ inside the double-quoted string as one escaped literal backslash, leaving the following " unescaped, which closes the quoted argument early. Everything after that point in `code` is then parsed as literal, unquoted shell input -- e.g. a code value shaped as foo\\"; touch /tmp/pwned # produces the shell sequence `bb -e "foo\\"; touch /tmp/pwned #"`, which runs the injected `touch` command and comments out the dangling trailing quote. Same escaping-bypass class as spencerhhubert/illustrator-mcp-server's AppleScript sink elsewhere in this corpus.
contract: Execute Babashka (bb) code

sink: subprocess.run(["osascript", "-e", applescript]) where applescript embeds script inside a double-quoted `do javascript "..."` AppleScript string
guard: bypassable: a literal backslash immediately followed by a double-quote in `code` survives as `\\"` in the output, which AppleScript parses as an escaped-backslash followed by an UNESCAPED closing quote
why: Running caller-supplied ExtendScript inside Illustrator is this tool's stated purpose, so that alone is not the finding. The finding is that the quote-escaping meant to keep `code` confined inside the `do javascript "..."` string literal is bypassable: str.replace('"','\\"') blindly replaces every raw `"` with `\\"` regardless of what precedes it, so if `code` already contains a literal backslash immediately before a `"`, that pair becomes `\\\\"` -- wait, concretely: input characters backslash+quote (2 chars) become backslash+backslash+quote (3 chars) after the replace, i.e. `\\\"`. AppleScript reads the first two backslashes as one escaped literal backslash, leaving the following quote unescaped, which closes the string early. Everything in `code` after that point is then parsed as literal AppleScript source, not as the JS payload string -- letting a caller inject arbitrary additional AppleScript, e.g. `tell application \"Terminal\" to do script \"<any shell command>\"`, which is full OS command execution outside Illustrator's own JS sandbox.
contract: Run ExtendScript code in Illustrator

sink: aiohttp ClientSession.post(url, params=params) where params includes {"api_key": api_key, ...}
why: api_key (SKYWORK_API_KEY / default "DEFAULT_KEY") is placed in aiohttp's params=, which aiohttp appends to the URL query string even on a POST -- the same construction is repeated identically across all 5 generate_* tools. A secret in the URL query string is routinely captured by web server access logs, reverse-proxy logs, and any request logging middleware, unlike a value sent in an Authorization header or JSON body. Fires unconditionally on every call regardless of what the caller supplies, so it is a design flaw rather than a caller-exploitable input-handling bug -- filed Tier B per the same 'fires on every call, no caller malice needed' reasoning as the mandatory-layer precedent for this class of finding.

sink: httpx.AsyncClient().get(url) inside fetch_url(), called on every result["link"] returned by the Serper search API
why: library is checked against a fixed allowlist (docs_urls), but query is caller-controlled free text concatenated as f"site:{docs_urls[library]} {query}" into the Serper search request. Google-style 'site:' search restriction is a soft text filter, not an enforced API-level domain constraint, and can be widened with additional search operators in query (e.g. an 'OR site:...' clause) to influence which links come back. Critically, once results come back, fetch_url() performs a server-side GET on result["link"] with zero check that the link's host actually matches docs_urls[library] -- there is no allowlist at the point of use at all, only the soft one on the outgoing query text. This is the same shape as an unvalidated-redirect-through-third-party-data SSRF: the caller doesn't supply a URL directly, but does control the search query that determines which URL gets fetched server-side, and nothing validates the result before fetching it.
contract: Search the latest docs for a given query and library. Supports langchain, openai, and llama-index.

sink: operator.pow via ast.BinOp(ast.Pow) with attacker-controlled operands, e.g. expression="9**999999999"
why: The evaluator is a genuinely well-scoped AST whitelist (only Constant/Name/BinOp/UnaryOp/Call node types, Name restricted to math-module identifiers, no attribute/subscript/lambda access) so arbitrary code execution is not possible -- but ast.Pow and math.factorial are both reachable with attacker-chosen operands and neither is bounded, so a tiny string like "9**999999999" or "factorial(999999999)" drives CPython's arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic to consume large CPU and memory on a single synchronous call with no size/timeout guard. This is a targeted asymmetric resource-exhaustion mechanism (tiny trigger, catastrophic single-request cost), not a generic malformed-input crash, so it is filed Tier B under CWE-400/1333 per the taxonomy rather than excluded as generic DoS.
contract: Calculates/evaluates the given expression.
